title: Generated Columns
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Generated Columns.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to generated expressions.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Generated Columns. Its primary job is to help you define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing generated columns teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: define and evolve schemas with constraints, generated values and changes that are safe for populated tables. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Generated Columns
content_blocks.code:
CREATE TEMP TABLE cart_line_demo (quantity integer NOT NULL, unit_price numeric(8,2) NOT NULL, line_total numeric(10,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (quantity * unit_price) STORED);
INSERT INTO cart_line_demo (quantity, unit_price) VALUES (3, 2.50) RETURNING quantity, unit_price, line_total;
content_blocks.expected_output: Returns quantity=3, unit_price=2.50 and generated line_total=7.50.
content_blocks.safety_note: Creates a temporary table and inserts synthetic data.
content_blocks.run_instructions: PostgreSQL 18 supports generated columns; this example explicitly uses STORED. Run in a disposable session.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.schema_assumptions: PostgreSQL 18 supports generated columns; this example explicitly uses STORED. Run in a disposable session.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: PostgreSQL 18 makes VIRTUAL generated columns the default; explicitly distinguish VIRTUAL from STORED and check version-specific restrictions. Compare the exact syntax and behavior with the PostgreSQL 18.6 generated-column documentation.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Generated Columns”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Generated expressions”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Generated expressions”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Generated Columns, with an explanation of “Generated expressions”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.
